t: Minimum Size Subarray in Infinite Array — Prefix Hash over Two Copies
o: We need the shortest window in the infinite repetition of `nums` whose sum equals `target`. Any window shorter than two full copies of `nums` looks like `j` full cycles plus a contiguous piece of `nums+nums`, so its length is `j*n + L`. In example 1 (`target=5`, cycle sum 6) the answer uses `j=0` and the piece `[2,3]`; in example 2 likewise `j=0`. Constraints (`n ≤ 1e5`, `target ≤ 1e9`) forbid simulating the infinite array, but sums are positive, so prefix sums plus a hash map find the shortest piece with any required sum in O(n).
k: Any candidate window decomposes into j full cycles plus a subarray of nums+nums, so only j = q and q-1 (q = target // sum(nums)) need checking.
All elements are positive, so both prefix-hash and sliding-window searches give the minimal piece length in linear time.

a.n: Approach 1: Prefix-sum hash map on nums+nums
a.i: Build prefix sums of two concatenated copies and record the first index of each prefix value. For a required remainder `need`, a subarray with sum `need` ending at r starts right after the first occurrence of `pref[r+1]-need`. Trying `j = q` (need = remainder) and `j = q-1` (need = remainder + total) covers the optimum.
s: Compute total = sum(nums), q = target // total, and prefix sums of nums+nums with first-occurrence map.
Define shortest(need) = minimal window length in nums+nums with sum need via the map.
Answer = min over j in {q, q-1} (j >= 0) of j*n + shortest(target - j*total).
a.t: O(n) per checked remainder, O(n) overall — two linear scans over 2n prefixes
a.sp: O(n) — prefix array and hash map

a.n: Approach 2: Sliding window instead of hash map
a.i: Since all values are positive, for each required remainder a classic two-pointer sweep over `nums+nums` finds the minimal window with that exact sum, avoiding the hash map.
s: For need in {remainder, remainder + total}, run a two-pointer window keeping sum <= need.
Record the minimal window whose sum equals need.
Combine with cycle counts q and q-1 as in Approach 1.
a.t: O(n) — constant number of linear two-pointer sweeps over 2n elements
a.sp: O(n) — the doubled copy of nums

w: Use the sliding-window version in an interview: it is simpler to reason about thanks to positivity. Pitfalls: forgetting the q-1 candidate (windows straddling more than one boundary), using int for prefix sums (they reach ~2e10), and returning -1 only after checking both remainders. Follow-ups: what if nums contained negatives (then only the prefix-hash works), or if you needed the count of windows rather than the minimum length.
